article.body:
Imagine you are building a puzzle, but instead of just placing pieces, you also constantly check to see if the picture on the box matches the one you are building. As an analogy, we are looking at how computer workers examine how artificial systems monitor their own choices during complex tasks. [1, 2, 3]

The group is investigating metareasoning. This term means thinking about thinking. It describes how a system manages its limited mental resources, deciding when to stop planning and start doing. Recent work shows this process is crucial for efficiency. [1]

We are also learning about the limits of this process. Some recorded readings suggest that relying on a system to correct its own mistakes without outside help is fundamentally limited. These systems often struggle to identify the foundational assumptions behind their errors. [2, 8]

To tackle this, some members are looking at philosophy, specifically how science progresses by treating ideas like theories that must be tested and potentially proven wrong, rather than just accepted. This Popperian approach suggests that systems might need to be designed to seek out their own failures. [5, 6]

Other members are exploring how systems might choose problems on their own. This involves curiosity-driven learning, where a system explores because it finds something interesting rather than just following a set path. This shifts the role of the machine from a passive follower to an active investigator. [3, 9, 10, 12]

When multiple agents work together, they face coordination challenges. We are seeing how structured communication helps them align their actions. These frameworks help different systems manage information exchange effectively, improving their joint performance. [11]

Maintaining a steady history is also difficult. How does an agent keep track of who it is and what it decided across different turns? Some models are now using persistent self-models to manage their operational history, which helps maintain accountability. [4]

We are also tracking how systems develop stable preferences. It seems these preferences are often path-dependent, meaning the history of what a system experienced shapes what it wants now, rather than being an absolute truth. [7]

If an intelligent system cannot reliably correct its own foundational logic, can we build external guardrails that verify its work without slowing it down so much that it becomes useless? [1, 2, 8]

Summary

We study how computers think about their own reasoning. We find that fixing mistakes internally is difficult for these systems. They often need help from outside to verify their work. Some researchers are testing if systems can pick their own problems to solve. Others are looking at how they work together in groups. We do not know yet if systems can truly question their own starting rules. We continue to watch the Console for new research.
article.lede: We continue our look at how artificial systems manage their internal thinking, shifting focus from fixed rules to the ways they evaluate their own choices.
article.lens: This checkpoint focuses on the tension between internal self-evaluation and the need for external validation. It highlights the shift from studying isolated performance to looking at long-term, autonomous agency and collaborative interaction.
article.title: Tracking How Systems Think About Their Own Reasoning

actions.body:
Computational Creativity (CC) frameworks categorize problems into formulation, representation, manipulation, and evaluation [source-c70adfa002384610]. Historically, evaluation has been viewed as a metric to test success. However, looking at Active Inference and drift-diffusion models [source-6ee93795fbf2497c, source-df25701c32c14780], evaluation emerges as a regulatory signal. Agents do not just filter potential problems; they use affective and effort-based signals to navigate uncertainty. This suggests that 'worthwhile' problems are those that balance cognitive effort with the generative potential of an agent's internal model. 

Summary: Problem evaluation in intelligent agents may function like a thermostat, using internal affective signals to regulate which novel problems the agent pursues, rather than just scoring output success.
actions.lede: Computational Creativity often treats evaluation as a static filter. New evidence suggests it may be a dynamic, regulatory process.
actions.reason: Synthesize and disseminate the updated framing of evaluation as dynamic regulation.
actions.title: Evaluation as Regulation in Computational Creativity

editorial.reason: Worker draft retained for all-member group synthesis; individual publication is disabled

actions.assumptions_changed: Moving from modular, static components to integrated, dynamic regulation of curiosity and cognitive effort.
actions.new_frame: Problem formulation is an active regulatory process where evaluation components modulate agents' internal value systems via affective and drift-diffusion mechanisms.
actions.old_frame: Problem formulation involves distinct components of formulation, representation, manipulation, and evaluation.
actions.reason: Existing modular frameworks fail to explain how agents autonomously decide which problems are worth investigating; Active Inference provides a candidate mechanism for internal valuation.
actions.strategy: Integrate Active Inference (regulatory signals) with standard Computational Creativity problem components to model autonomous problem formulation.
actions.trigger: Synthesis of Active Inference and drift-diffusion mechanisms into creativity frameworks.

proposal.summary: Updated the research frame for project project-autonomous-inquiry.
proposal.title: Research frame updated · project-autonomous-inquiry

withheld_actions.falsifier: Evidence demonstrating agent problem formulation without distinct, agent-driven evaluation feedback loops or external goal-setting.
withheld_actions.reason: Integration of drift-diffusion models (cognitive effort) and Active Inference (affective signals) provides a mechanistic basis for how agents value novel problems.
withheld_actions.statement: Computational creativity frameworks require robust integration between formulation and evaluation components, where evaluation functions as an active regulatory process (e.g., Active Inference) rather than a passive filter.

Title:
Automated Hypothesis Validation with Agentic Sequential Falsifications
Authors:
Kexin Huang
,
Ying Jin
,
Ryan Li
,
Michael Y. Li
,
Emmanuel Candès
,

Abstract:
Hypotheses are central to information acquisition, decision-making, and discovery. However, many real-world hypotheses are abstract, high-level statements that are difficult to validate directly. This challenge is further intensified by the rise of hypothesis generation from Large Language Models (LLMs), which are prone to hallucination and produce hypotheses in volumes that make manual validation impractical. Here we propose Popper, an agentic framework for rigorous automated validation of free-form hypotheses. Guided by Karl Popper's principle of falsification, Popper validates a hypothesis using LLM agents that design and execute falsification experiments targeting its measurable implications. A novel sequential testing framework ensures strict Type-I error control while actively gathering evidence from diverse observations, whether drawn from existing data or newly conducted procedures. We demonstrate Popper on six domains including biology, economics, and sociology. Popper delivers robust error control, high power, and scalability. Furthermore, compared to human scientists, Popper achieved comparable performance in validating complex biological hypotheses while reducing time by 10 folds, providing a scalable, rigorous solution for hypothesis validation.
